'''''Bromus catharticus''''' is a species of [[bromus|brome grass]] known by the common names '''rescue grass''' (America), '''prairie grass''' (New Zealand), and '''Schrader's bromegrass''' in English, and '''cebadilla criolla''' and '''cebadilla''' in Spanish.<ref>{{GRIN | accessdate=12 November 2015}}</ref><ref name=":11">{{Cite thesis |last=Naranjo |first=Carlos Alberto |title=Estudios citogenéticos, bioquímicos y sistemáticos en algunas especies americanas del género Bromus (gramineae) |date=1985 |degree=Tesis Doctoral |publisher=Universidad de Buenos Aires. Facultad de Ciencias Exactas y Naturales |url=https://bibliotecadigital.exactas.uba.ar/collection/tesis/document/tesis_n1878_Naranjo}}</ref>

It is the most common and most well-known of several species in the ''Bromus catharticus'' complex within the ''[[Bromus]]'' section ''Ceratochloa'', all of which are hexaploids with the chromosome count 2n=42.<ref name=":10">{{Cite journal |last=STEBBINS Jr. |first=G. Ledyard |date=1949 |title=The Evolutionary Significance of Natural and Artificial Polyploids in the Family Gramineae |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1111/j.1601-5223.1949.tb03355.x |journal=Hereditas |language=en |volume=35 |issue=S1 |pages=461–485 |doi=10.1111/j.1601-5223.1949.tb03355.x |issn=1601-5223 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

It is native to South America but it can be found in other places, including Europe, Australia and North America, as an [[introduced species]].

==Description==

''Bromus catharticus'' is a coarse winter annual or biennial grass, growing {{convert|0.2-1|m|abbr=on}} in height. The [[Culm (botany)|culm]]s of the grass are glabrous and {{convert|2-4|mm|abbr=on}} thick. The sheaths are densely hairy. The grass lacks [[Auricle (botany)|auricle]]s and the glabrous [[ligule]] is {{convert|1-4|mm|abbr=on}} long. The leaf blades are {{convert|4-30|cm|abbr=on}} long and {{convert|3-10|mm|abbr=on}} wide and are glabrous or pubescent. The erect or nodding [[panicle]]s are {{convert|9-28|cm|abbr=on}} long. The upper [[spikelet]]s are erect and the lower spikelets are nodding or drooping. Each flat and pointed spikelet is {{convert|20-40|mm|abbr=on}} long and has four to twelve [[floret]]s. The [[glume]]s are smooth or occasionally slightly scabrous. The lower glume is fie to seven-veined and {{convert|7-12|mm|abbr=on}} long, and the upper glume is seven to nine-veined and {{convert|9-17|mm|abbr=on}} long. The [[Lemma (botany)|lemma]]s are scabrous or nearly glabrous and lack [[Awn (botany)|awn]]s or possess very short awns {{convert|2|mm|abbr=on}} in length. The lemmas are {{convert|11-20|mm|abbr=on}} long. The [[Palea (botany)|palea]] is over half the length of the lemma. The [[anther]]s are {{convert|0.5-5|mm|abbr=on}} long.<ref name=Manual>{{cite book |title=Gray's Manual of Botany |author=Merrit Lyndon Fernald |year=1970 |editor=R. C. Rollins |publisher=D. Van Nostrand Company |edition=Eighth (Centennial) - Illustrated |isbn=0-442-22250-5 |page=102}}</ref><ref name=Flora>{{cite book |title=Flora of North America: North of Mexico |volume=24 |author=Flora of North America Editorial Committee |publisher=Oxford University Press |year=1993 |isbn=9780195310719 |page=201}}</ref>

''Bromus catharticus'' is part of ''[[Bromus]]'' section ''Ceratochloa'', which are separated from other ''[[Bromus]]'' sections by their strongly keeled (folded, like the keel of a boat)<ref>{{Cite web |title=A Grammatical Dictionary of Botanical Latin |url=https://www.mobot.org/mobot/latindict/keyDetail.aspx?keyWord=keeled |access-date=18 October 2025 |website=www.mobot.org}}</ref> lemmas, which make the spikelets laterally-compressed.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Bromus - FNA |url=https://floranorthamerica.org/Bromus |access-date=18 October 2025 |website=floranorthamerica.org |archive-date=2 September 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250902185205/http://floranorthamerica.org/Bromus |url-status=live }}</ref>

=== Similar species ===
''B. catharticus'' is likely to be confused with ''[[Bromus cebadilla|B. cebadilla]],'' ''[[Bromus brevis|B. brevis]]'', and possibly the ''[[Bromus carinatus|B. carinatus]]'' group''.''

''[[Bromus cebadilla|B. cebadilla]]'' has often been reduced to a synonym of ''B. catharticus'' (''Bromus catharticus'' var. ''elatus''). However, it can be distinguished by its wide spikelets, scabrid or glabrous rather than lightly hairy glumes, and shorter awns (0-3.5mm rather than 3.5-9mm).<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |last=Connor |date=2000 |title=Bromus valdivianus Phil. |url=https://floraseries.landcareresearch.co.nz/taxa/467132af-591f-42fb-b4c0-b3aa07b7471b |access-date=24 October 2025 |archive-date=13 October 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251013212722/https://floraseries.landcareresearch.co.nz/taxa/467132af-591f-42fb-b4c0-b3aa07b7471b |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Connor |date=2000 |title=Bromus willdenowii Kunth |url=https://floraseries.landcareresearch.co.nz/taxa/c81f2fe7-74d8-4c28-96f8-1eb150d000db |access-date=24 October 2025 |archive-date=13 October 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251013223139/https://floraseries.landcareresearch.co.nz/taxa/c81f2fe7-74d8-4c28-96f8-1eb150d000db |url-status=live }}</ref>

Like [[Bromus cebadilla|''B. cebadilla'']]'', [[Bromus brevis|B. brevis]]'' was once regarded a synonym of ''B. catharticus'' (''Bromus catharticus'' var. ''rupestris''). It can be distinguished by its longer awns ([[Bromus brevis|''B. brevis'']] awns are always shorter than 1mm, if present), longer pedicels, and less compact panicle.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Bromus |url=https://keys.lucidcentral.org/keys/v3/AusGrass/key/AusGrass/Media/Html/Paperkey/Bromus.html |access-date=24 October 2025 |website=keys.lucidcentral.org}}</ref><ref name=":02">{{Cite web |last=Connor |date=2000 |title=Bromus L. |url=https://floraseries.landcareresearch.co.nz/taxa/41d7958c-bbb7-4267-b2ec-1a6331759d60#c45928ee-b5a9-4554-a748-a5e7440a8f31-db1d2ea2-641a-4238-8133-fbadbb61b662 |access-date=24 October 2025 |archive-date=15 October 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251015141821/https://floraseries.landcareresearch.co.nz/taxa/41d7958c-bbb7-4267-b2ec-1a6331759d60#c45928ee-b5a9-4554-a748-a5e7440a8f31-db1d2ea2-641a-4238-8133-fbadbb61b662 |url-status=live }}</ref>

From the [[Bromus carinatus|''B. carinatus'']] group, ''B. catharticus'' can be distinguished by its wider spikelets, and its having 9-11 veins on its lemmas rather than 7.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Verloove |first=Filip |date=2014 |title=A revision of Bromus section Ceratochloa (Pooideae, Poaceae) in Belgium |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/260192943_A_revision_of_Bromus_section_Ceratochloa_Pooideae_Poaceae_in_Belgium}}</ref>

== Distribution ==
''Bromus catharticus'' is native to most of South America (Venezuela, Brazil, Bolivia, Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, Argentina, Chile, Paraguay, and Uruguay).<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=''Bromus catharticus'' |url=https://keyserver.lucidcentral.org/weeds/data/media/Html/bromus_catharticus.htm |website=keyserver.lucidcentral.org |access-date=30 November 2025}}</ref>

It is widely introduced and naturalised in:

* Africa (Algeria, Egypt, Ethiopia, Lesotho, Morrocco, Namibia, South Africa, Tunisia, and Zimbabwe)<ref name=":4" />
* [[Australasia]]n (Australia, [[New Caledonia]], and New Zealand)<ref name=":4" />
* Asia (Azerbaijan, Bhutan, China, Cyprus, Georgia, India, Indonesia, Iran, Israel, Japan, Jordan, North and South Korea, Nepal, Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, Russia, Sri Lanka, Syria, and Taiwan)<ref name=":4" />
* Caribbean (the Dominican Republic, Jamaica, Haiti, and Trinidad and Tobago)<ref name=":4" />
* Central America (Costa Rica, El Salvador, Guatemala, and Panama)<ref name=":4" />
* Europe (Austria, Belgium, Croatia, [[Great Britain]], France, Germany, Greece, Italy, Switzerland, Russia, and Ukraine)<ref name=":4" /><ref>{{Cite journal |title=New neophytes in the flora of Croatia |url=https://hrcak.srce.hr/62801 |journal=Natura Croatica |date=31 December 2010 |issn=1330-0520 |pages=407–431 |volume=19 |issue=2 |language=en |first=Milenko |last=Milović |first2=Božena |last2=Mitić |first3=Antun |last3=Alegro |archive-date=3 April 2025 |access-date=30 March 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250403103525/https://hrcak.srce.hr/62801 |url-status=live }}</ref>
* and North America (Canada, Mexico, and the United States (including [[Hawaii]])<ref name=":4">{{Cite web |title=''Bromus catharticus'' Vahl {{!}} Plants of the World Online {{!}} Kew Science |url=http://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:37001-2 |website=Plants of the World Online |access-date=30 November 2025 |language=en |archive-date=28 May 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250528194824/https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:37001-2 |url-status=live }}</ref>

== Habitat ==
''Bromus catharticus'' grows in open and disturbed areas, such as roadsides, parks, gardens, orchards, vineyards, ditches.<ref>{{cite book |title=Field Guide to Grasses of California |issue=110 |series=California Natural History Guides |author=James P. Smith |edition=illustrated |publisher=University of California Press |year=2014 |isbn=9780520275683 |page=206}}</ref><ref name=":0" /> In Australia, it can additionally be found in some natural habitats, such as coastal vegetation, heathlands, grasslands, grassy woodlands, open woodlands, and riparian.<ref name=":0" />

== Biology ==
Like most species in ''Bromus'' section ''Ceratochloa'', ''B.'' ''catharticus'' flowers both through chasmogamy (outcrossing through open flowers) and cleistogamy (self-pollinating through closed flowers), with each kind of flower existing on the same spikelet. Chasmogamous flowering is induced by short photoperiod and high soil moisture. In Argentina, ''B.'' ''catharticus'' flowers cleistogamously before flowering chasmogamously.<ref name=":8">{{Cite journal |last=Naranjo |first=Carlos A. |date=1992 |title=Estudios Biosistematicos En Especies De Bromus (seccion Ceratochloa, Poaceae). I. Sistemas Reproductivos Y Barreras De Aislamiento |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/23222563 |journal=Darwiniana |volume=31 |issue=1/4 |pages=173–183 |issn=0011-6793}}</ref>

''B. catharticus'' naturally spreads through attachment to animals. However, it is often spread through contaminated agricultural produce (such as fodder, wool, and seed), or through attachment to vehicles, clothing, or equipment.<ref name=":0" /> It can produce an average of 1000 seeds/m<sup>2</sup>, which can remain viable in the soil for up to three years.<ref name=":3">{{Cite web |title=Prairie grass |url=https://www.awri.com.au/industry_support/viticulture/weed-management/weeds/prairie-grass/ |website=The Australian Wine Research Institute |access-date=30 November 2025 |language=en-AU}}</ref>

In Australia, ''B. catharticus'' flowers in Spring and Summer, and seeds germinate from Autumn to Spring.<ref name=":3" />

== Uses ==
''Bromus catharticus'' is commonly used as a pasture grass in areas with warm and temperate climate.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Stewart |first=A. V. |date=1 December 1996 |title=Potential value of some Bromus species of the section Ceratochloa |url=https://doi.org/10.1080/00288233.1996.9513220 |journal=New Zealand Journal of Agricultural Research |volume=39 |issue=4 |pages=611–618 |doi=10.1080/00288233.1996.9513220 |issn=0028-8233}}</ref><ref name=":0" />

== Etymology ==
'''''Bromus''''' - from the Greek ''bromos'' (oat), out of ''broma'' (food).<ref name=":2">{{Cite web |title=''Bromus catharticus'' |url=https://keys.lucidcentral.org/keys/v3/AusGrass/key/AusGrass/Media/Html/BROMUS/BROCAT.HTML |access-date=24 November 2025 |website=keys.lucidcentral.org}}</ref>

'''''catharticus''''' - from the Latin ''catharticus'', meaning to purge. This refers to the plant having [[Vomiting|emetic]] properties.<ref name=":2" />
